headlines.article_text: Palantir (PLTR) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palantir reported Q3 earnings that topped Wall Street's estimates. U.S. commercial revenue more than doubled and surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time. The company has seen a boost from heightened demand for artificial intelligence tools. In this article PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:24 01:24 Palantir beats on earnings and revenue, Q3 commercial revenue surpasses government revenue Closing Bell: Overtime Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools. Shares dipped about 4% in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : 44 cents adjusted vs. 41 cents expected Revenue : $2.31 billion vs. $2.18 billion expected Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share. "I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople. Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years. Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability. In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity . "My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here." Palantir stock chart. Apple shares fell when the company said that it expected total company revenue to grow between 7% and 10% on an annual basis in the December quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were expecting growth equivalent to 11.4%. Here's how the company did compared to analysts' estimates, according to LSEG. Revenue increased 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier, Apple said in a statement on Monday. Apple's iPhone revenue in the quarter only included eight days of new Phone 18 Pro sales. And Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the period was over. Monday's report includes a full quarter of higher-priced Apple products, as the company raised prices across the board in June after it signaled challenges with memory supply and other parts. Apple increased prices on iPhones by $100. The iPhone maker is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a rush for computer components. Apple said on Monday that its memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period. Still, Ternus said in a statement that Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." Ternus told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came in spite of supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "I think at this point, with everything we've achieved, it just feels like we've never been more confident that the best is yet to come," Ternus said. Ternus said that Apple "reluctantly" raised prices, which helped it offset component increases. Apple said tariff refunds added 5 cents to earnings per share. Monday's earnings call, set to start at 5 p.m. ET, will be the first with Ternus as CEO. Investors want to hear from him about the company's plans in China after its AI software got approved, as well as the slew of recent product launches and how the company continues to grapple with global shortages of memory and flash storage. headlines.summary: Intel’s turnaround now hinges on proving its foundry strategy can deliver, as customers look for signs the company will add fab capacity and catch TSMC
headlines.article_text: Intel foundry faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel's 29% drop on Friday left the stock down 45% in October, its worst month on record, according to FactSet. Intel sees the global market for server CPUs growing fivefold to $200 billion in the next five years, but the softening PC market is hurting legacy revenue. Intel is redirecting some 18A capacity in Oregon fabs to make Intel 3 chips for its server CPUs In this article INTC TSM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel Corp. CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the company's event in Tokyo, Japan, Oct. 7, 2026. Akio Kon | Bloomberg | Getty Images As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground. It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products. Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations. Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade. The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading. Intel vs. Nasdaq since start of October Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industrywide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales. That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, used for its data center products. Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said. Intel didn't respond to a request for comment. Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta 's Muse. Competitor or partner? As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview. "If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip. Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters. watch now VIDEO 16:50 16:50 Can Intel’s New Arizona Chip Fab Bring It Back From The Brink? Tech Intel's 18A chips, for its own use, are in high-volume production out of Arizona, with a second fab in the works. A first structural truss was just installed at Intel's new Ohio facility, although the project is nearly five years behind schedule . Another roadblock to getting new customers, Yoffie said, is that chipmakers like Broadcom and Qualcomm may hesitate to manufacture chips at a company that's also a competitor on the product side. "The right solution is for Intel to spin off the foundry business," Yoffie said, calling it "not only the best solution, but maybe the only solution." Klein said AMD is likely the only major chipmaker that isn't interested in manufacturing at Intel because the two companies compete directly in the CPU market. He called it a "competitive, secrecy, privacy issue." AMD reports third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. Yoffie said the U.S. needs Intel to succeed. "Ultimately, TSMC can only create maybe 20-25% of their global capacity in the United States and that will still take several years," he said. "If we have no American foundry and we run into any number of geopolitical problems, supply chain problems like we had under Covid, that is going to be bad for the country and bad for the American semiconductor industry." Greg Abbott remains favored to defeat his Democratic opponent state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to prediction market traders, but his odds have slipped. Many are watching Texas to see if voters deliver a blow to data center development, which Abbott previously supported before turning more skeptical on the industry this year. Hinojosa has attacked Abbott for his previous support of data centers. Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, left, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa. Getty Images Political observers are watching the Texas gubernatorial election for signs of an artificial intelligence data center backlash in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, and prediction market traders see growing odds of the Democratic candidate pulling off an upset. Gov. Greg Abbott , a Republican seeking a fourth term, has a 60% chance of beating Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to speculators on platform Kalshi. Hinojosa's odds to win have jumped from 8% in mid-July to 40% on Monday, with many of those gains coming in recent weeks as a series of polls have shown the race to be tightening . Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls. Hinojosa is seeking to be the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than 30 years. She has used Abbott's previous support for data center development in the state as an attack against the incumbent . In November 2025, Abbott touted a $40 billion investment by Google — which included bringing three new data center campuses to the state — by saying that Texas will be the "epicenter of AI development." But Abbott has changed his tune as voters' opinion of data centers has soured over the past year. Abbott in August ordered an audit of data centers that sought to connect to the state's grid, and then in September he halted the approval of all data center-related permits until an audit of the existing waitlist is conducted. Hinojosa is running on an immediate data center moratorium until the legislature puts guardrails on the industry, according to her campaign website. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. In this article ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Oracle's one-day performance The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026 While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting. headlines.article_text: Marvell to buy Lumentum in all-stock deal Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Marvell will acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction. The deal will expand Marvell's push into optical connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026. In this article MRVL LITE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:41 04:41 Marvell CEO Matt Murphy on Lumentum deal: We're creating the 'category leader in AI connectivity' Squawk on the Street Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm.
